The first survey of Hollow Valley was commissioned in the spring of 1849, after a dispute over grazing rights had dragged on for three seasons. The county hired a young engineer named Abel Marsh, who arrived with two assistants, a brass theodolite, a set of sixty-six foot chains, and a notebook bound in oilcloth. The instructions he received were simple enough: walk every boundary, record every corner, and set a stone at each place where the line turned. What the instructions did not say was how much of the valley lay under water in April, or how quickly the weather could turn on the upper slopes.

Marsh began at the old mill and worked north along the stream, taking bearings at every fence corner and noting the height of each bank above the water line. His assistants carried the chains through alder thickets and across meadows that had not been grazed since the previous autumn. Twice the party lost a day to rain, and once they lost a stone marker to a farmer who insisted that the boundary had always run along the hedgerow rather than the ditch.

By midsummer the survey had reached the northern ridge. From there the view opened over the whole valley, and Marsh could see the fields, the orchards, and the scattered farmhouses whose boundaries he had spent four months recording. He wrote in his notebook that the upper meadows were drier than anyone had claimed and that the old maps were wrong by as much as a furlong in places. The final map, drawn over the winter, showed the distance between the two great oaks at the valley mouth as just under half a mile, a figure that later surveyors confirmed to within a few feet.

The county accepted the map without argument, and for the next forty years it served as the record of every fence, lane, and drainage ditch in the valley. Marsh never returned. He took a post with the railroad and spent the rest of his career laying out grades through country far steeper than anything he had walked that summer.
